clue.text: Small timepiece's piece of cloth

parts.note: S is the size printed on a clothing label for small
a watch is the timepiece you wear on your wrist

explanation.walkthrough: The trap is reading 'Small timepiece' as one idea. 'Small' stands alone as its abbreviation, and the apostrophe-s that looks possessive is only the joint between wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A swatch is the sample square a tailor or decorator snips from a fabric to show it, so it is exactly a small piece of cloth.

clue.text: Encircles tree with garbage including carbon, depression begins now

definitions.note: The setter defines an event by the headline it produced rather than by a noun phrase, so the definition is a whole sentence where the answer is a thing.

indicators.note: To include something is to take it in and hold it there, so the single letter for the element is dropped inside the word for rubbish rather than tacked onto either end.

parts.note: a hedge that encircles a field walls it in
the word goes in at face value, four letters off the page
trash is the American word for household garbage
C is carbon's symbol in the periodic table, and it lands after the first letter of the rubbish

explanation.walkthrough: 'Depression' offers a dip in the ground or a low mood long before it offers the economic one. Every join lands in the wrong place on purpose: the T that ends the middle word is the front of the rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1929 crash on Wall Street is the event conventionally dated as the start of the Great Depression, so the definition names it by what followed.

clue.text: Time we rode off, Rose

indicators.note: Milk that has gone off has turned, and letters told to turn do not stay in the sequence the clue printed them in.

parts.note: T is the standard abbreviation for time, as on a stopwatch
the six letters of these two words, resettled in a new order

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' looks like the woman being addressed as the riders leave, and the capital letter is the setter helping that along. It is the past tense of rise.
explanation.definitionFit: To tower over something is to stand high above it, so in the past tense the two words describe the same upward reach.

clue.text: Mineral-rich fluid tumbling earthward

indicators.note: Something that tumbles falls over itself end for end, so it lands in a different arrangement from the one it set out in.

parts.note: the nine letters of this single word, dealt out again

explanation.walkthrough: Fluid tumbling earthward is rain, which is what the surface wants you to picture. The one word that looks like scenery is the whole of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard water is groundwater that has taken up dissolved calcium and magnesium from chalk or limestone, which is what makes it mineral-rich.

clue.text: Discriminating announcement of just one summary

indicators.note: An announcement is made out loud, so what the clue hands over is the sound of the words rather than their spelling.

parts.note: just one of a thing is a single one of it, and the indefinite article is the one-letter way of saying so
the gist of a report is its summary, and spoken straight on from the article those two words make a single six-letter sound

explanation.walkthrough: 'Discriminating' is praise when you say it of a palate and an accusation here — that flip is the whole misdirection, and only the ear gets you from two words to one.
explanation.definitionFit: Discriminating carries the unkind sense of treating people differently, and the answer names someone who does that on the grounds of how old you are.

clue.text: A doctorate describing Citizen's second cause of Rosebud's loss

indicators.note: In geometry you describe a circle around a shape by drawing it round the outside, which is what these letters do to the one that follows.

parts.note: the article is taken at face value

indicators.note: It picks a letter out by position rather than by meaning: the one standing second in the word, counted from the front.

parts.note: a PhD is the doctorate, and here it is split open to make room
the italics point at Citizen Kane, and it is the second letter of that first word that is wanted

explanation.walkthrough: Rosebud is the sled in the film, so the surface is all cinema. The garden reading is the one that counts: a rosebud lost off its bush.
explanation.definitionFit: Aphids are the greenfly that colonise a rose bush and suck the sap, so one of them is what costs a gardener the bud.

clue.text: Trade barrier: flickering amber, then green light

indicators.note: A flickering light will not hold steady, and neither will the letters it is pointing at.

parts.note: the five letters of the traffic light's middle colour, rearranged
green is the signal to go, and giving something the green light is telling it to proceed

explanation.walkthrough: The whole surface is a set of traffic lights, which is the joke: what gets built out of them is the opposite of permission to proceed.
explanation.definitionFit: An embargo is an official ban on trading with a country, so it is literally a barrier laid across trade.

clue.text: Drops chaps after reshuffle: poor!

indicators.note: A cabinet reshuffle keeps every minister and gives them all new jobs, which is exactly what happens to these fifteen letters.

parts.note: fifteen letters across three words, dealt out again

explanation.walkthrough: 'After' looks like an instruction to put the chaps behind the drops. It is fodder, and every letter of all three words goes into the pot.
explanation.definitionFit: Strapped for cash is the idiom for having no money to hand, and poor is the plain adjective for the same condition.

clue.text: Elbow rather jittery: make things easier

indicators.note: Somebody jittery cannot keep still, and letters that cannot keep still do not stay where the clue put them.

parts.note: eleven letters from these two words, redealt

explanation.walkthrough: 'Elbow' is a body part in the surface and raw material in the parse. The idiom comes from the high jump, where the bar drops to make the clearance easy.
explanation.definitionFit: Lowering the bar is setting a standard people can clear more easily, so the phrase and the definition describe the same slackening.

clue.text: Shoe quiz

definitions.meaning: in Britain this is the flat, soft-soled shoe worn for gym or for dancing
to question somebody persistently is to work information out of them, the way water is drawn from a well

explanation.walkthrough: A two-word clue is all definition and no wordplay, so the only thing to find is where one meaning stops and the next one starts.
explanation.definitionFit: A pump is the light flat shoe used for gym or dancing in Britain, and to pump somebody is to press them for information.

clue.text: Australian drunk disembarked

parts.note: A is the short form of Australian that crosswords keep permanently on hand
lit is old slang for drunk — lit up, like a Christmas tree

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' is the anagram indicator that isn't. Nothing here is jumbled: it is a plain synonym, and the tipsy Australian of the surface does all the misleading.
explanation.definitionFit: To alight from a train or bus is to step down out of it, which is what disembarking is; the word survives on British station announcements.

clue.text: Some of bosun's crew edgy, ready to take off

indicators.note: It asks for a part rather than the whole, and the part wanted is a run of letters already lying untouched in the words that follow.

parts.note: nine consecutive letters begin at the fourth letter of the first word and stop two short of the end of the last

explanation.walkthrough: Hidden words like to run straight across an apostrophe, because the eye reads possession instead of letters. 'Ready to take off' sounds like an aeroplane and describes a lid.
explanation.definitionFit: A lid or a fitting that has been unscrewed is loose and ready to be lifted away, so taking off here means removal rather than flight.

clue.text: Disgust: social outcast returns

indicators.note: Somebody who returns comes back along the road they went out on, so the letters are read from the far end towards the near one.

parts.note: a leper is the byword for somebody society will not go near, and those five letters are then read the other way round

explanation.walkthrough: 'Disgust' is the verb here, not the noun — you repel somebody the way a smell disgusts them. The outcast wanted is the figurative leper, not the medical one.
explanation.definitionFit: To repel is to drive someone back in revulsion, and to disgust is that same act named by the feeling it produces.

clue.text: Precious-ish, emeraldesque rock in demand; olivine trinket, primarily!

definitions.text: Precious-ish, emeraldesque rock in demand; olivine trinket, primarily!

indicators.note: What comes primarily comes before all else, so each word gives up only the character it opens with.

parts.words: Precious-ish, emeraldesque rock in demand; olivine trinket
parts.note: the opening letter of each of these seven words, read in the order they stand

explanation.walkthrough: An all-in-one: the sentence describes the gem and spells it at the same time, and the exclamation mark is the setter enjoying that. 'Emeraldesque' was invented for the job.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: peridot is the green gem variety of olivine, near-precious rather than precious, and cut for costume jewellery.

clue.text: Launch campaign?

definitions.meaning: to throw something forward — the same root that gives a missile its name
a piece of organised work with an aim and an end date

explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions and no wordplay. The question mark owns up to the second one being loose: a campaign is a kind of the thing rather than another word for it.
explanation.definitionFit: To project is to throw forward, which is what launching does, and a project is equally an undertaking of the sort a campaign is.

clue.text: Say conga is agreed policy

definitions.meaning: a conga is danced in single file, each dancer holding the hips of the one in front

indicators.note: It means 'for instance', flagging that what follows is one example of the thing wanted rather than another name for it.

definitions.meaning: the position a political group has settled on and expects its members to repeat

explanation.walkthrough: The same two words carry a dance floor and a party conference. 'Say' is the tell: it warns you that a conga is an instance, not a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A party line is the position a political party requires its members to hold, and a conga is literally a line of people at a party.

clue.text: Overnight train: what it will cross

definitions.meaning: the service with berths, taken so the journey happens while you are asleep
the timber or concrete beams laid crosswise under the rails, holding them to gauge

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue turns on 'it' — the train from the first half. Americans call those beams ties, which is why the second definition has to describe rather than name.
explanation.definitionFit: One word covers both the berth train and each beam laid across the track bed, so the train literally runs over what it is named after.

clue.text: Upset, Everyman cut 50% of fats, being staunch

indicators.note: In a down clue what is upset reads from the bottom of the column upwards, so the assembly is taken in the opposite of the order it was built.
It halves the word that follows, and the half kept is the back one — the opening pair is what gets cut away.

parts.note: the setter signs the puzzle Everyman, and a setter pointing at themselves in the wordplay is two letters
the back half of a four-letter word, its first two letters gone

explanation.walkthrough: 'Staunch' looks like the adjective for a loyal supporter and is the verb for stopping a flow. Everyman appearing in person is a habit of this setter worth banking.
explanation.definitionFit: To stem a flow and to staunch a wound are the same act: holding back something that is running, so both verbs mean to stop it.

clue.text: Lighter, twinkling, somewhere in Sicily

parts.note: a lighter shade of a colour is a paler one
in a twinkling means in a moment, and moment is shortened to two letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lighter' is doing its colour job, not its flame job, and 'twinkling' is time rather than starlight — the surface offers the wrong sense of both at once.
explanation.definitionFit: Palermo is the capital and largest city of Sicily, so the definition places it by island and leaves the name for you to supply.

clue.text: Snubs enthusiasts for Bible study

parts.note: RE is religious education, the scripture lesson on a British school timetable
a buff is an enthusiast — a film buff, an opera buff

explanation.walkthrough: Everything after the first word reads as one phrase, enthusiasts for Bible study, and the parse cuts it in two with the school subject coming first.
explanation.definitionFit: To rebuff somebody is to turn their approach away curtly, which is what snubbing them amounts to.

clue.text: Dumb row's erupting, cancelling some characters — 23?

indicators.note: Crossing letters out at each end leaves the ones you keep sitting exactly where they were, in the order they were printed.

parts.note: seven consecutive letters begin at the last letter of the first word and run through the second into the third

explanation.walkthrough: 'Erupting' pulls hard towards a jumble, or towards an upward move in a down clue, and it is neither: those letters sit still. The 23 points at another entry.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition is the answer at 23, which is one make of browser — a definition by example, with the question mark owning up to it.

clue.text: Pest — and missing — neither good nor bad

indicators.note: What is missing is not there, so the word it names is struck out of the longer phrase before you read what remains.

parts.note: an irritating person is a so-and-so, the polite British way of not naming them
the linking word in the middle of that phrase is quoted here so that it can be lifted out

explanation.walkthrough: The dashes read as a parenthesis in a grumble about pests, and what they really fence off is an instruction. Britain's mildest insult stands in for a name you would rather not say.
explanation.definitionFit: So-so is the shrug between the two extremes — not one nor the other — which is the middle ground the definition spells out.

clue.text: We hear 40 in Rome go far

indicators.note: Hearing rather than reading is the point: what the clue names is to be said out loud and the sound of it written down.

parts.note: Roman numerals put X for ten in front of L for fifty to mean fifty less ten
those two numerals read out as the names of their letters make a five-letter word

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here is Italian. The numeral is not translated but spoken, letter name by letter name, which is the whole trick, and 'go far' means getting on in life.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody who excels goes far in the sense of outdoing the field, not in the sense of covering distance.

clue.text: Frequently depressed characters?

parts.note: the surface offers low spirits; the sense in play is the physical one, pushed down under a finger
not people of a gloomy sort but letters and symbols, one printed on each of the things pressed

explanation.walkthrough: There is nothing to take apart, only one phrase read twice. The office gloom of the surface turns into fingers on plastic, and the question mark is the setter admitting it.
explanation.definitionFit: Every key carries a character and is pressed down all day, so the clue describes the object by what happens to it rather than naming it.

clue.text: Two knights on the street; one's a rascal

indicators.note: In a down clue what sits on something else is written above it, so what follows this word goes underneath.

parts.note: chess writes a knight as N, while a knighthood is a K — one of each, and no repetition
AVE is how an avenue is shortened on a street sign

explanation.walkthrough: Two knights and two different abbreviations — the setter is not asking for the same letter twice. 'One's' does nothing but hold the sentence upright.
explanation.definitionFit: Knave is the old word for a dishonest man, and the playing card between ten and queen took its name, so rascal is the plain modern equivalent.

clue.text: Composed acid satire initially attacking Balkans' neighbour

indicators.note: To compose is to put pieces together into an arrangement of your own, so these letters are yours to set in a fresh order.

parts.note: ten letters from these two words, waiting to be redealt

indicators.note: It asks for the beginning of the word it governs — the opening letter only, and nothing after it.

parts.note: the opening letter of this word, and the eleventh letter the enumeration asks for

explanation.walkthrough: 'Composed' means calm in the surface, where a cool reviewer writes a sharp notice, and means assembled in the parse. That double life is the standard anagram misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: The Adriatic washes the western shore of the Balkan peninsula, so the sea and the region are neighbours along a coastline.

clue.text: Classic car's finish: Switzerland, then major Italian city

parts.note: CH is Switzerland's international vehicle code, short for the Latin Confoederatio Helvetica
the Italian capital, and the four-letter city this description is pointing at

explanation.walkthrough: 'Finish' looks like an instruction to take a last letter, which is the trap. It is a noun here — the shiny plating itself — and the colon marks the only break.
explanation.definitionFit: Chrome is the bright plating that trims a classic car's bodywork, so 'finish' here means a surface coating and not an ending.

clue.text: Mostly clear: thyme's not refined

indicators.note: Most of a thing is some of it and not all, which is a loose way of saying the letters already sit inside the words that follow.

parts.note: six consecutive letters begin at the third letter of the first word and stop three short of the end of the second

explanation.walkthrough: 'Not refined' invites you to rough up the letters of thyme's. It is the definition instead, and nothing is jumbled: the surface only pretends to be a weather forecast.
explanation.definitionFit: Earthy means coarse or unpolished — an earthy sense of humour is the unrefined kind — so the definition is a plain negative.
